subject: computing
subtitle: Types of cyber threats including malware, phishing, social engineering, and denial of service attacks.

data.targetWord: an umbrella term for any software specifically designed to disrupt, damage, or gain unauthorised access to a computer system

examples.en-GB: Viruses, worms, ransomware, and spyware are all types of malware.

data.targetWord: malware that attaches itself to a legitimate file and spreads when an infected file is shared or opened, requiring human action to propagate

examples.en-GB: A virus hidden inside an email attachment spreads to new computers when recipients open the infected file.

data.targetWord: self-replicating malware that spreads automatically across networks without any user action, exploiting vulnerabilities in software

examples.en-GB: The WannaCry worm spread automatically across NHS networks in 2017 without any staff clicking anything.

data.targetWord: malware disguised as legitimate, useful software that once installed opens a backdoor giving attackers remote access to the system

examples.en-GB: A free video player download that secretly installs a backdoor is an example of a Trojan horse.

data.targetWord: malware that encrypts all the victim's files so they cannot be opened, then demands a payment (usually in cryptocurrency) in exchange for the decryption key

examples.en-GB: Ransomware locked hospital computers during the WannaCry attack, making patient records completely inaccessible.

data.targetWord: malware that secretly monitors user activity — recording keystrokes, capturing screenshots, and tracking browsing — then sends stolen data to the attacker

examples.en-GB: Spyware on a laptop recorded every password typed and silently sent them to the attacker's server.

data.targetWord: malware that displays unwanted advertisements and redirects browser searches to advertising websites, often bundled with free software

examples.en-GB: After installing a free download, adware began showing pop-up adverts and redirecting every web search.

data.targetWord: a social engineering attack using fake emails or websites that mimic trusted organisations to trick users into revealing login credentials or other sensitive information

examples.en-GB: A phishing email pretending to be from Apple asked users to click a link and enter their password on a fake website.

data.targetWord: a phishing attack carried out via SMS text messages, typically containing a malicious link or a request to call a fake number

examples.en-GB: A smishing message claimed a parcel could not be delivered and asked the recipient to pay a fee via a suspicious link.

data.targetWord: a phishing attack carried out over the telephone, where the attacker impersonates a bank, government department, or tech support to extract sensitive information

examples.en-GB: A vishing call pretended to be from a fraud department, pressuring the victim to reveal their banking PIN.

data.targetWord: manipulating people psychologically into revealing confidential information or performing actions that compromise security, exploiting human trust rather than technical vulnerabilities

examples.en-GB: Social engineering attacks target people rather than software, as humans are often the weakest link in any security system.

data.targetWord: an attack that floods a web server or network with so many fake requests that it cannot respond to legitimate users, effectively taking the service offline

examples.en-GB: A denial of service attack against a bank's website made it impossible for customers to log in for several hours.

data.targetWord: a denial of service attack coordinated from thousands or millions of compromised devices simultaneously, making it much harder to block than a standard DoS attack

examples.en-GB: The DDoS attack used a botnet of 500,000 hijacked devices to flood the gaming server with traffic.

data.targetWord: an attack that systematically tries every possible combination of characters until the correct password is found

examples.en-GB: A brute force attack on a short, simple password can crack it in seconds using automated software.

data.targetWord: an attack where malicious SQL code is entered into a web form so that it gets executed by the database, allowing the attacker to read, modify, or delete data

examples.en-GB: An SQL injection attack on a shopping website exposed the usernames and passwords of all registered customers.

data.targetWord: an attack where the attacker secretly intercepts and can read or alter communications between two parties who believe they are communicating directly

examples.en-GB: On an unencrypted public Wi-Fi network, a man-in-the-middle attack can intercept login details sent to a website.

data.targetWord: a low-tech attack where the attacker physically watches a victim enter their password, PIN, or other sensitive information

examples.en-GB: At an ATM in a busy street, shoulder surfing allowed a criminal to see the PIN of the person in front of them.

data.targetWord: a social engineering technique where an attacker uses a fabricated story or false identity to persuade someone to hand over information or access

examples.en-GB: Blagging involved the attacker calling a bank and pretending to be a colleague to obtain a customer's account details.

data.targetWord: a social engineering attack in which the attacker creates a fabricated backstory to manipulate a target into revealing information or granting access

examples.en-GB: Pretexting: a caller claimed to be an IT technician who needed the employee's password to fix a network problem.

data.targetWord: a network of computers and devices that have been infected with malware and are secretly controlled by an attacker to carry out coordinated attacks

examples.en-GB: The botnet of 100,000 infected home routers was used to launch a DDoS attack on a major website.

data.targetWord: a hidden method of bypassing normal authentication to gain remote access to a computer system, often installed by a Trojan

examples.en-GB: The Trojan installed a backdoor that let the attacker access the victim's computer remotely at any time.

data.targetWord: a highly targeted form of phishing where the attacker researches the specific victim and personalises the attack using real details such as their name, employer, or colleagues

examples.en-GB: A spear phishing email addressed the target by name and mentioned their manager, making it much harder to identify as fake.

data.targetWord: a software update released by a developer to fix known security vulnerabilities and bugs in a program or operating system

examples.en-GB: WannaCry exploited a Windows vulnerability that had already been fixed by a security patch — organisations that had not applied it were attacked.

data.targetWord: a security system requiring users to verify their identity using two or more different methods, such as a password plus a code sent to a phone

examples.en-GB: Even if an attacker discovers your password, multi-factor authentication blocks them because they also need your phone to receive the verification code.

data.targetWord: security software or hardware that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks connections that do not meet defined security rules

examples.en-GB: The firewall blocked the worm's attempt to spread to other computers on the school network.

data.title: Put these steps in the correct order to show how a phishing attack unfolds:
items: The attacker creates a fake email mimicking a trusted organisation such as a bank
The fake email is sent to thousands of potential victims
A victim receives the email and is convinced by its appearance
The victim clicks the malicious link in the email
The victim is taken to a fake website that looks identical to the real one
The victim enters their username and password on the fake site
The attacker captures the credentials and gains unauthorised access to the victim's real account

data.title: Put these steps in the correct order to show how a ransomware attack progresses:
items: The victim receives a phishing email containing a malicious attachment or link
The victim opens the attachment or clicks the link, executing the ransomware
The ransomware begins silently encrypting all files on the device and any connected drives
A ransom message appears on screen, stating that files are encrypted and demanding cryptocurrency payment
The victim must decide whether to pay the ransom or restore from backups
If backups exist, files can be restored; if not, the victim may lose their data permanently

pairs.text: Virus — attaches to files and spreads when a user shares the infected file
Trojan — user installs it thinking it is legitimate software
Adware — user installs free software that bundles the adware
Worm — exploits network vulnerabilities and replicates across networks
WannaCry — spread itself across the NHS network with no staff involvement
